title: Fructose Emerges as Unexpected Driver of Cancer Metastasis in New Study
excerpt: Researchers at The Wistar Institute found that fructose released by chemotherapy-surviving cancer cells acts as a signal for tumors to spread, raising questions about diet's role in cancer progression.
body:
• Cancer cells that survive chemotherapy release fructose, which signals neighboring tumor cells to detach and spread throughout the body.
  • Fructose suppresses cholesterol production in cancer cells, weakening the "cellular glue" that holds tumors together and enabling metastasis.
  • Mice fed a high-fructose diet developed more widespread metastatic disease even without chemotherapy, suggesting dietary fructose alone may influence cancer progression.
  • The findings are preclinical and have not been confirmed in humans, but researchers are exploring an FDA-approved diabetes drug that may block the mechanism.

A study from The Wistar Institute at the University of Pennsylvania has identified fructose — the sugar found in fruits, honey, and high-fructose corn syrup — as a previously unrecognized driver of cancer metastasis. Published in Nature Aging in July 2026, the research reveals how cancer cells that survive chemotherapy use fructose to help tumors spread.

How Surviving Cancer Cells Weaponize Sugar

The research team, led by senior author Katherine Aird and first author Aidan Cole, focused on ovarian cancer treated with cisplatin, a widely used platinum-based chemotherapy. While cisplatin kills many cancer cells, some survive by entering a state called cellular senescence — they stop dividing but remain biologically active.

These senescent cells, it turns out, don't just sit quietly. They release a cocktail of molecules that reshape the tumor environment. When the researchers collected this molecular mixture and exposed untreated cancer cells to it, those cells didn't divide faster. Instead, they loosened their grip on neighboring cells and began to detach — the critical first step in metastasis.

"As far as we know, this is the first time anyone has shown, in a preclinical model rather than just a dish, that it's the molecules these cells release — not the cells themselves — that drive the cancer's spread."

— Aidan Cole, postdoctoral fellow, The Wistar Institute

Through metabolic analysis and a CRISPR screen, the team pinpointed fructose as the key messenger. Senescent cells consumed glucose but secreted elevated levels of fructose, effectively converting one sugar into another to fuel metastasis.

The Cholesterol Connection

The mechanism works through cholesterol. Fructose alters mitochondrial metabolism in neighboring cancer cells, ultimately suppressing cholesterol production. Cholesterol acts as biological glue, helping stabilize cell membranes and anchor cells to one another. With less cholesterol, cancer cells become less adhesive and more likely to break free and spread.

This finding carries an unsettling implication for the 39 million Americans who take statins. These cholesterol-lowering drugs, prescribed to prevent heart disease, reduced the cellular adhesion in the researchers' experiments, promoting the same kind of cell escape that fructose triggered.

"We haven't tested this effect in patients yet, but it raises questions about combining cholesterol-lowering drugs with chemotherapy, especially since ovarian cancer is most common in postmenopausal women who are often already on statins," Aird told Medical News Today.

Diet Alone May Matter

Perhaps the study's most striking finding: dietary fructose can drive metastasis even without chemotherapy. Mice fed a high-fructose diet developed more widespread cancer than those receiving glucose. When researchers disabled the cancer cells' ability to metabolize fructose, fewer cancer cells migrated.

High-fructose corn syrup accounts for 8% to 20% of daily caloric intake for some Americans. A third of U.S. teenagers consume 15% or more of their calories as sugar, much of it as fructose, according to federal data.

"Fructose may play an underappreciated role in modulating tumor cell behavior. This raises the possibility that restricting fructose intake could be a promising dietary intervention to assist in treatment response."

— Study authors, Nature Aging

Beyond Ovarian Cancer

The researchers believe the mechanism may extend to other cancers. "We think other cancers that spread within the torso — pancreatic, colon, liver — could behave similarly," Aird said. A separate 2025 study from UT MD Anderson Cancer Center found that the glucose-fructose combination in sugary drinks fueled colorectal cancer metastasis through a related enzyme pathway, and Washington University researchers demonstrated that fructose processed by the liver promotes tumor growth across multiple cancer types.

What This Means Going Forward

The Wistar team is already pursuing follow-up work. They are testing an FDA-approved diabetes drug that may block fructose production by chemotherapy-surviving cells, and they plan to collaborate with physicians to study whether dietary intake correlates with patient outcomes.

Medical experts urge caution about drawing clinical conclusions from preclinical data. Ami Vaidya, co-chief of gynecologic oncology at Hackensack University Medical Center, called the fructose finding "the most striking discovery" but emphasized that these findings "require further validation in human studies before clinical applications can be considered." Patients should continue following their oncology team's guidance, she said, while the science catches up to the question of whether what we eat could change how cancer spreads.
